Radar altimeters measure ocean surface wind speed and significant wave height by analyzing radar cross section and return pulse broadening.
The radar cross section (RCS) is sensitive to surface roughness on the scale of the radar wavelength (~2 cm for Geosat).
Significant wave height (SWH) is proportional to the surface mean-squared slope (MSS) of ocean waves.
The study used 236 pairs of buoy and Geosat altimeter wind speed measurements for regression analysis.
Buoy wind speeds are 8.5-minute averages normalized to 10 m height above the surface.
Multiple linear regression was applied to test if adding RCS and SWH reduces residual errors in wind speed retrieval.
The smoothed-Brown (SB) algorithm showed a 2% residual error reduction when RCS was included, with 99% confidence.
The Chelton-Wentz (CW) algorithm did not significantly improve with the addition of RCS alone.
Including SWH improved both SB and CW algorithms with confidence levels above 75%.
Using 'excess SWH' with the CW algorithm yielded a 98% confidence level in residual reduction.
Differences between buoy and altimeter wind speeds arise from spatial-temporal sampling differences and instrument limitations.
Wind-wave growth is suppressed by preexisting swell, affecting altimeter wind speed estimates.
Geosat altimeters operate at about 13.5 GHz with a radar wavelength near 2.2 cm.
The altimeter range precision is approximately 3 cm for Geosat.
Maximum spatial and temporal separation allowed between buoy and altimeter data pairs were 50 km and 30 minutes respectively.
The Pierson-Moskowitz wind-wave spectrum was used as a baseline for expected SWH.
The study suggests that including SWH and RCS can marginally improve wind speed retrieval algorithms but larger datasets are needed for conclusive results.
Radar altimeter return pulse shape changes due to ocean wave crests and troughs cause pulse broadening used to estimate SWH.
The frictional wind speed u* relates to the momentum transfer from wind to ocean surface and influences MSS and RCS.
